summary.title: What is "good taste" in software engineering?
summary.one_liner: Good engineering taste is the ability to pick the right set of engineering values for a specific project, and it differs from technical skill.
keywords: map and filter vs for loop
how to develop good taste in programming
takeaways: Technical taste is distinct from technical skill: you can have strong skill with poor taste, or weak skill with good taste.
Taste is your ranking of engineering values (resiliency, speed, readability, correctness, flexibility, portability, scalability, development speed), and the right ranking depends on the project.
Mature engineers weigh the benefits of each option in the specific case instead of treating one approach as always best.
Bad taste usually comes from inflexibility, such as applying 'best practice' or favourite tools regardless of fit.
Good taste shows up as projects succeeding over varied kinds of work, and it is developed by working on varied problems while staying flexible.
summary.summary: The author argues that technical taste is the ability to choose the engineering values that fit a given project, and that it is separate from technical ability. He lists values such as resiliency, speed, readability, correctness, flexibility, portability, scalability and development speed, and says an engineer's taste is set by which of these they rank highest. He describes bad taste as inflexibility, using the 'broken compass' analogy, and suggests good taste can be judged by whether projects succeed across varied domains. The post is an opinion essay with footnotes and no code or tutorial steps.
